findings.title: Forwarder signs the outgoing HTLC before the link is durable
findings.source: security audit OMN-NEW-002, verified against source at 8fa26907
findings.summary: forwardIncoming calls addHTLC (which reserves WOTS keys and signs the new state), writes the updated channel into the channel map, builds the link record, and only then calls linkJournal.record(). A crash or a storage failure between the signed state and the journal write leaves an outgoing obligation with no durable incoming-to-outgoing association.
findings.impact: Stranded liquidity and broken backward settlement after a restart: the relay knows it signed an outgoing HTLC on-chain-ish state but cannot reconstruct which incoming HTLC it was forwarding. Contradicts the durability claim the recovery design rests on.

repro.expected: The association is durable before or atomically with the signed outgoing state, so recovery can always pair an outgoing HTLC with its incoming one.
repro.actual: record() runs after addHTLC() and after channels.set(); a failure in between is unrecoverable.
evidence: fix proposed in PR #218 (intent journaled before signing; recovery completes or drops it)
packages/omnia-relay/src/forwarder.ts:203 — addHTLC(outChannel, ...)
packages/omnia-relay/src/forwarder.ts:219 — options.channels.set(result.channel.channelId, result.channel)
packages/omnia-relay/src/forwarder.ts:231 — await options.linkJournal.record(link)

fix.approach: Write an intent record before signing (hashlock, incoming ids, planned outgoing channel/amount/timeout), then sign, then commit the outgoing htlc id. Recovery resolves intents: if the outgoing htlc exists, complete the link; if not, the intent is safe to drop.
constraints: Do not claim durability for a link that was not written before the signature.
Do not make the journal the authority for channel balances.
acceptance: A crash injected between signing and commit leaves a recoverable record.
recover() can reconstruct the link from the intent plus channel state.
Normal forwarding writes the same number of journal entries.

findings.title: Relay recovery discards a link when either side is terminal
findings.source: security audit OMN-NEW-003, verified against source at 8fa26907
findings.summary: recover() keeps a link only while both HTLCs are pending: terminal(inHtlc) || terminal(outHtlc) causes it to delete the link and remove it from the journal. An outgoing HTLC being fulfilled does not imply the incoming one was fulfilled — settling backwards is a separate later step — so the association is dropped at exactly the point it is still needed.
findings.impact: After a restart in the middle of a forward, the link needed to reveal the preimage to the incoming channel is gone. Liquidity on the incoming side stays locked until timeout, and the relay cannot prove the pairing.

repro.expected: A link is discarded only once the incoming HTLC is settled or the pair is provably unspendable.
repro.actual: terminal(outHtlc) alone deletes the link and its journal entry.
evidence: fix proposed in PR #218 (recovery keys on the incoming HTLC only)
packages/omnia-relay/src/forwarder.ts:289 — const terminal = (h) => !h || h.status !== "pending"
packages/omnia-relay/src/forwarder.ts:290 — if (terminal(inHtlc) || terminal(outHtlc)) ... remove(hashlock)

fix.approach: Split the terminal condition: an outgoing HTLC that is fulfilled means "reveal the preimage to the incoming side", not "done". Discard only when the incoming HTLC is settled or both sides are timed out.
constraints: Do not keep links forever: unresolved links must have a timeout-based exit.
Do not reveal a preimage without the corresponding fulfilled outgoing HTLC.
acceptance: recover() returns links whose outgoing HTLC is fulfilled and whose incoming HTLC is still pending.
Those links settle backwards after recovery.
A link whose incoming HTLC is settled is still removed.

findings.title: Both live splice paths omit chainProvider, so a broadcast splice is marked active with a placeholder coin
findings.source: security audit OMN-NEW-005, verified against source at 8fa26907
findings.summary: observeSpliceSuccessor exists precisely because the predecessor coin is spent and the successor must be found on chain. finalizeSplice only calls it when options.chainProvider is set; otherwise it defaults successorStatus to "active" and spliceFundingCoinId to `${txid}-0`, which is a placeholder. Both host call sites (prepared splice and direct splice) pass no chainProvider.
findings.impact: A splice is treated as confirmed before its successor coin exists. The channel is reported active with a coin id that is not a real output, restart recovery has nothing valid to resume from, and later operations can act on a channel that the chain does not have.

repro.expected: A spliced channel stays funding_pending until the successor coin is observed on chain.
repro.actual: Without chainProvider the branch is skipped and status is set to active immediately.
evidence: fix proposed in PR #218 (finalizeSplice defaults to funding_pending; both call sites pass a chain observer)
packages/omnia-host/src/api/methods.ts:1368 — finalizeSplice(..., { broadcast }) (no chainProvider)
packages/omnia-host/src/api/methods.ts:3076 — finalizeSplice(..., { broadcast, proposerLeaseProvider })
packages/omnia-splice/src/finalize.ts:345 — let successorStatus = "active"; only replaced inside if (options?.chainProvider)

fix.approach: Pass the host chain adapter at both call sites, and make the absence of a chainProvider an error rather than an implicit "assume active". Default to funding_pending when observation is unavailable.
constraints: Do not use `${txid}-0` as a funding coin id for any state that can be acted on.
Do not block the RPC indefinitely: observation stays bounded.
acceptance: Both call sites pass a chain provider.
finalizeSplice without observation yields funding_pending, never active.
A splice becomes active only after the successor is found with the required confirmations.

findings.title: withChannelLock only guards the direct pay path
findings.source: security audit OMN-NEW-007, verified against source at 8fa26907
findings.summary: withChannelLock is defined once and used exactly once, around the direct omniaPay RPC. HTLC operations, prepared submissions, settlement and splice paths do not take it, so they can read, modify and write the same channel concurrently.
findings.impact: Concurrent RPC or peer-driven operations can interleave read-modify-write cycles. The signing watermark blocks some conflicting signatures but does not serialize state derivation, so a lost update or a state built on a stale sequence is possible.

repro.expected: Every channel mutation, whatever its entry point, runs under one per-channel coordinator.
repro.actual: One use of withChannelLock, in the direct pay handler.
evidence: fix proposed in PR #218 (shared re-entrant per-channel lock across RPC and peer handlers)
packages/omnia-host/src/api/methods.ts:2025 — const withChannelLock = ...
packages/omnia-host/src/api/methods.ts:2408 — the only call site

fix.approach: Move the lock into the channel store or a mutation coordinator and take it in every path that mutates a channel: pay, HTLC add/reveal/timeout, prepared submit, settlement and splice, including peer handlers.
constraints: Do not rely on the watermark as the serialization mechanism.
Do not introduce a global lock that serializes unrelated channels.
acceptance: All mutation entry points acquire the same per-channel lock.
A concurrency test that interleaves two mutations yields a consistent sequence with no lost update.

findings.title: The watchtower is implemented and exported but never started by the host
findings.source: security audit OMN-NEW-008, verified against source at 8fa26907
findings.summary: createChannelWatchService exists with detection and retry logic and is exported from the package index, but no code calls it: createOmniaHost().start() contains no reference to it. Its close detection also keys on the original funding coin being spent, which cannot distinguish a unilateral close from an update or splice, and it adds the channel to a persistent closed set.
findings.impact: A host holding funds runs with no automated response to a unilateral close: no contest transaction is produced before the deadline. Where the service is used manually, a normal update can be misread as a close and suppress later events.

repro.expected: The host starts a chain-aware watcher that tracks successive channel coins and deadlines.
repro.actual: Only the definition and the export exist; lifecycle.ts has no watcher.
evidence: fix proposed in PR #218 (watch service started by the host; successor-aware close detection)
packages/omnia-host/src/watch.ts:69 — export function createChannelWatchService
packages/omnia-host/src/index.ts:50 — export only
packages/omnia-host/src/lifecycle.ts — no reference to the watch service

fix.approach: Start the watcher in host.start() and stop it in close(). Track the current channel coin per sequence rather than the original funding coin, distinguish update from close by the spending transaction, and handle reorgs and contest deadlines.
constraints: Do not treat "funding coin spent" as equivalent to "unilateral close".
Do not let the persistent closed set suppress later events for a channel that is still live.
acceptance: Host startup starts the watcher and shutdown stops it.
A simulated unilateral close triggers the contest path before the deadline.
A normal state update or splice does not mark the channel closed.

findings.title: Finalization guards validate identifiers, not the resulting state
findings.source: re-audit R-002, verified against source at 5d8c427b
findings.summary: CAN-007 stopped unsolicited finalizations by requiring a local acceptance. But assertSpliceFinalized checks ids (spliceId, channelId, splicedFrom, txId) and assertVcFinalized checks kind, factory and a one-step sequence. Neither compares balances, totalValue or allocations with the locally signed proposal. Separately, FACTORY_CLOSE_FINALIZED marks a known factory closed with no settlement check.
findings.impact: A counterparty can finalize a transition whose economic terms differ from what was accepted, as long as the identifiers line up. A factory can be marked closed without proof that settlement happened.

repro.expected: The finalized channel/factory is compared field-by-field with the accepted proposal, including balances, totalValue and allocations, and signatures over that state verify.
repro.actual: Only identifiers and the sequence step are compared.
evidence: packages/omnia-host/src/peer-guards.ts — assertSpliceFinalized compares ids and txId only
packages/omnia-host/src/peer-guards.ts — assertVcFinalized compares factoryId and sequence only
packages/omnia-host/src/lifecycle.ts:459-462 — FACTORY_CLOSE_FINALIZED sets status closed without settlement evidence

fix.approach: Pass the locally accepted proposal/acceptance into the guards and compare the complete finalized state (balances, totalValue, allocations, virtual-channel set) plus the signatures over it. Require settlement evidence before a factory is marked closed.
constraints: Do not weaken the existing id checks.
Do not accept a finalized state that differs in any economically meaningful field.
acceptance: A finalized splice with altered balances is rejected.
A VC finalization whose allocations differ from the signed plan is rejected.
FACTORY_CLOSE_FINALIZED without settlement evidence does not close the factory.

findings.title: Omnia writes atom amounts with MiniNumber scale 0, encoding channel values 10^44 times too large
findings.source: two-host S4 run (`openChannel` threw `Cannot convert 0.2 to a BigInt`) reviewed against minima-global/Minima `objects/Coin.java`, `objects/base/MiniNumber.java` and `objects/Transaction.java`
findings.summary: Minima has one amount type, `MiniNumber`: JSON reports it as decimal MINIMA text ("0.2"), while the binary transaction stores `(unscaled, scale)` with value = unscaled x 10^-scale. Omnia kept channel maths in atoms but its canonical serializer wrote atom integers with scale 0, so a 0.2 MINIMA channel was encoded as 2x10^43 MINIMA. Separately, the RPC provider normalised its coin amounts to atoms while Hosted, Lookup and Composite providers stayed decimal, so `ChainStateProvider.getCoins/getCoin` no longer had a single unit contract.
findings.impact: Every non-trivial channel funding/update/settlement draft was invalid: `Transaction.checkValid()` requires 0 < amount <= 1,000,000,000 and rejects the encoded value as an invalid Minima amount. The S4 run failed earlier, at `BigInt("0.2")`, which masked the encoding fault. Consumers that expected node decimal text (tx-builder coin selection and serialisation, the extension's `TOTEM_GET_COINS` and selection, edge-adapters and realtime balances) would have been inflated by 10^44 once a provider returned atoms; a composite fallback flipped the unit mid-application.

repro.command: build a funding draft for 0.2 MINIMA (`totalValue = 2e43` atoms) and decode the serialized coin amount: `buildFundingTx(...)` -> `omniaDraftToCanonicalMinimaBytes(...)`
repro.expected: input/output amount is `MiniNumber(unscaled = 2x10^43, scale = 44)`, which Java reads as 0.2 MINIMA and accepts.
repro.actual: the amount was written as `MiniNumber(unscaled = 2x10^43, scale = 0)`, which Java reads as 2x10^43 MINIMA; `isValidMinimaValue()` rejects it.
evidence: minima-global/Minima objects/Coin.java:239 — `amount` JSON is `mAmount.toString()` (decimal text)
minima-global/Minima objects/base/MiniNumber.java:31-49 — MAX_DECIMAL_PLACES = 44, MINI_UNIT = 1E-44
minima-global/Minima objects/base/MiniNumber.java:287-299 — binary form is [scale][length][unscaled]
minima-global/Minima objects/Transaction.java:165 — `isValidMinimaValue()` requires 0 < amount <= 1e9
packages/omnia/src/transactions.ts: serializeCoinForMinima wrote `writeMiniNumberLocal(opts.amount)` with the default scale 0
packages/chain-provider/src/providers/minima-rpc.ts: getCoins/getCoin returned atoms while hosted.ts and lookup-client.ts returned decimal

fix.approach: Define one contract: providers return node-native decimal text; `@totemsdk/core` owns `amountToAtoms`/`atomsToAmount`/`coinAmountAtoms`; Omnia converts once at its boundary and writes every coin amount as `MiniNumber(unscaled = atoms, scale = 44)`. Value-bearing program state ports use the same scale and the scale is bound into the signed state commitment, so a signer cannot re-encode a port at scale 0. The Rust/WASM mirror uses arbitrary-precision integers and the same scale rules.
constraints: Do not normalise units inside one ChainStateProvider implementation; the interface has one unit.
Do not write atom amounts with scale 0 anywhere.
Bind the state-port scale in the commitment; a signed state must not be re-encodable at a different scale.
acceptance: getCoins/getCoin return decimal text from every provider and a composite fallback cannot change units.
A 0.2 MINIMA funding draft decodes to scale 44 with value 0.2 and passes the Java validity bound.
Value-bearing state ports round-trip at scale 44; counters/sequences stay scale 0.
Rust/WASM digest and commitment parity hold.

findings.title: Factory opening requests the funding signature before the proposal exists (regression from CAN-010)
findings.source: re-audit R-003, verified against source at 5d8c427b
findings.summary: prepareFactory builds the plan and immediately sends FACTORY_FUNDING_REQUEST; FACTORY_PROPOSAL is only sent later by submitFactory (and by createFactoryMethod after its own signer call). CAN-010 now requires the receiver to hold an accepted factory with a matching pendingCommitment before it will sign, which cannot be true yet. The two changes contradict each other, so a fresh two-host factory opening fails at the funding step.
findings.impact: Factory opening is blocked on the prepared path and likely on the createFactory path. This is a functional regression introduced by the CAN-010 fix, not a pre-existing defect.

repro.expected: prepare → sign → finalize completes against a second host.
repro.actual: The responder answers ERROR ("does not match any locally accepted factory") because it has not received the proposal yet.
evidence: fix proposed in PR #222: both host paths send FACTORY_PROPOSAL first and use the acceptance as the funding witness
packages/omnia-host/src/api/methods.ts:1455-1473 — funding request inside prepareFactory
packages/omnia-host/src/api/methods.ts:1574 — FACTORY_PROPOSAL sent later in submitFactory
packages/omnia-host/src/api/methods.ts:2752 — createFactory method requests the signature before its proposal too
packages/omnia-host/src/peer-guards.ts:57-89 — resolveFactoryFundingTarget requires an accepted factory

fix.approach: Reorder both flows so the proposal (with funding materials) establishes the pending factory before any funding signature is requested, and use the responder opening signature over the same commitment as the funding witness instead of a second round. Add a FACTORY_FINALIZED follow-up so the responder learns the funding txid after the proposer broadcasts.
constraints: Do not relax CAN-010 back into an unbound signing oracle.
Do not allow a second FACTORY_PROPOSAL to re-sign after acceptance.
acceptance: A two-host prepare → sign → finalize run completes and both sides hold the same funding txid.
An unsigned/unknown digest is still refused.

findings.title: Hawk 0.3.0 cannot complete mainnet IBD: block proofs rejected, blocks skipped, tip parks ~1,000 behind
findings.source: live run 15 Nov 2026: mainnet node on host A (us-east-1), 0.3.0 vs 0.2.12
findings.summary: A fresh Hawk 0.3.0 node on mainnet (no -test, no -solo) syncs to block 2,418,985 and then loops on "Invalid MMR Proof! @ 2418985", never advancing and never binding the RPC port. The 0.2.12 release, started on the same host minutes later, completed IBD to block 2,421,050 via cascade with zero MMR errors.
findings.impact: The canary gate requires Hawk 0.3.0 (exact match), so no live scenario can run against the current build on mainnet. Factory, channel and settlement evidence cannot be produced until 0.3.0 syncs or the gate is given a documented exception.

repro.expected: The node reaches /readyz 200 on mainnet and the run proceeds.
repro.actual: readyz stays 000; the log repeats "Invalid MMR Proof! @ 2418985" for the same block indefinitely.
evidence: root cause 4 (residual 171->998 MMR lines at the tip): checkMMR validated a block's own witness proofs against the parent MMR. Blocks that carry their own coin set (superblocks) can never match it; the block's coin set is bound by its own MMR root, which checkTxPoWBlock/blockStateMatches rebuild and compare. Skipping the per-proof check for blocks (transactions stay strict) gives 0 MMR lines in 150s while the chain advanced 6 blocks, versus ~3/min before

root cause 3 found: checkTxBlockOnly compares the block difficulty against a trailing average over the local tree, which cannot match for a historical IBD block. Block 2420149 failed with "Incorrect TxPoW block difficulty" and everything after was skipped for a missing parent
with all three fixes the same build synced from scratch on mainnet to block 2421363 against a peer top of 2421362, syncing 0, zero difficulty rejections (171 residual MMR lines, non-blocking)
experiments rejected: reverting tx_pow_tree to 0.2.12 (sort order + side-branch collection) still parks at 2420225 and raises MMR errors to 754; setSyncIBD call sites are identical in both versions
residual is in IBD peer/response selection: the node loops asking a peer whose batch top (2420114) is below its own tip (2420148) and discards the blocks as historical; IBD_LIMIT_MINS is new in 0.3.0

root cause 2 found: the one-greeting-per-connection guard (new in 0.3.0) returns early on the duplicate, suppressing the IBD retry that 0.2.12 used to obtain its cascade. With the guard relaxed a fresh node logged Cascade: Loading 3361 nodes within a minute and reached the cascade tip with 0 MMR errors

both fixes are on minima-more PR #2; residual: after adopting the cascade the node sits at the cascade tip and loops requesting IBD at tip-1, receiving batches that end below its tip and are ignored as historical
after threading the offset through checkTxPoWSimple for transactions inside a block: still parks, this time at 2420143 with 411 MMR errors, readyz 200, syncing 0, ~1090 blocks behind the peer
hundreds of "SyncBlock missing parent (skipping, not fatal)" lines: the tree is rebuilt from a subset, so the batch top is never reached and the IBD loop finishes early

with the block-proof offset fix (minima-more PR #2): 0 Invalid MMR Proof, RPC binds, but the node then stalls at "No TxPoWTree yet.. required for NIO_SYNCTXBLOCK" and never receives a cascade; readyz stays 503 after 13 minutes
0.2.12 on the same host logs "Cascade: Loading 3361 nodes" and reaches block 2421050
0.3.0: peer ahead top=2421118, IBD requested, tip stuck at 2418985, RPC never bound
0.3.0 log: 200+ lines of "Invalid MMR Proof! @ 2418985", tip unchanged for >3 minutes
0.2.12 on the same host: readyz 200, block 2421050, syncing 0, 0 MMR errors, ~2 min via cascade

witnessesMatch (blockStateMatches) verifies coin proofs with parentMMR.checkProof because block proofs are one block ahead, but the sync path calls checkTxBlockOnly/checkTxPoWSimple first, which use checkProofTimeValid against the parent MMR

fix.approach: Make the sync-block path use the same one-block-ahead proof semantics that blockStateMatches already uses, for the block TxPoW and any local transaction bodies, instead of checkProofTimeValid against the parent MMR. Then re-run mainnet IBD on a clean data dir and require the tip to track the peer.
constraints: Do not disable the witness gate by default to hide this: IBD_WITNESS_CHECK is already false.
Do not weaken blockStateMatches while fixing the earlier check.
acceptance: A fresh 0.3.x node on mainnet reaches readyz 200 and tracks the peer tip across a cascade boundary.
No "Invalid MMR Proof" loop at any height.
verification: hawk-node: start on mainnet with a clean data dir and watch /readyz and the tip

findings.title: Liquidity-bond passes an atom count as the verifier's decimal claimedAmount, rejecting every pool deposit
findings.source: omnia-host pool test against the real deposit path (`depositToPool` -> `verifyDeposit`)
findings.summary: `VerifyDepositParams.claimedAmount` is decimal MINIMA text (chain-provider compares it with the node's decimal `coin.amount`). liquidity-bond built it from `commitment.amount.toString()`, and `commitment.amount` is an atom count, so the omnia-host verifier converted it to atoms a second time. A 100000 MINIMA deposit became 1e93 atoms at the comparison.
findings.impact: Every non-zero liquidity-pool deposit failed the amount gate with "insufficient amount", and `acceptLiquidityCommitment`/`confirmLiquidityCommitment` refused to accept or confirm funding. The failure looked like a funding problem, not a unit bug.

repro.expected: a commitment for a funded coin of 100000 MINIMA passes on-chain verification.
repro.actual: `insufficient amount`: coinAmountAtoms(coin) = 1e49 vs amountToAtoms("1" + 49 zeros) = 1e93.
evidence: packages/liquidity-bond/src/commitment.ts:59,123,162 — `claimedAmount: commitment.amount.toString()`
packages/liquidity-bond/src/types.ts:256 — `amount: bigint` (atoms)
packages/chain-provider/src/types.ts:83 — `claimedAmount` is decimal text
packages/omnia-host/src/api/methods.ts — verifier compares `coinAmountAtoms(coin)` with `amountToAtoms(request.claimedAmount)`

fix.approach: Render the commitment amount as decimal text at the verifier boundary with `atomsToAmount(commitment.amount)`; keep the verifier contract decimal and the internal ledger in atoms.
constraints: Do not change `VerifyDepositParams.claimedAmount` to atoms; it compares against the node's decimal `coin.amount`.
Do not weaken the amount gate.
acceptance: A 100000 MINIMA pool deposit verifies and is accepted.
An under-funded coin still fails.
The omnia-host pool lifecycle test passes unchanged in assertions.

findings.title: mintVtxo replaces the pool commitment root with a single-leaf tree
findings.source: Omnia whole-family re-audit (2026-11-17), finding OMN-002
findings.summary: mintVtxo builds its proof set from `[vtxo]` and assigns that single-leaf root to `pool.commitmentRoot`. The pool type holds no membership set and the mint does not advance epoch or batchId, so a second mint replaces the root and the first VTXO no longer verifies against the pool.
findings.impact: Previously minted claims stop verifying against the pool root. Any verifier that anchors on the current root rejects legitimate holders; there is no epoch history to fall back to.

repro.expected: After minting A then B, A and B both verify against the pool root the operator publishes.
repro.actual: pool.commitmentRoot equals the root of B alone; A's proof points at the earlier root.
evidence: packages/omnia-vtxo/src/vtxo.ts: mintVtxo `buildVtxoProofSet([vtxo])`
packages/omnia-vtxo/src/types.ts: OmniaVtxoPool has commitmentRoot but no membership set

fix.approach: Decide the contract first: either commitmentRoot covers the whole active set (the pool carries the member leaves and mint rebuilds the tree) or it covers one epoch (mint advances epoch/batchId and the epoch journal is the authority for historical proofs). Implement the chosen contract atomically and record it in docs.
constraints: Do not silently keep the single-leaf root — it makes the field mean something different from its name.
Existing VTXO ids and leaves must not change.
Epoch roots must remain verifiable after later mints.
acceptance: Two sequential mints leave both proofs verifiable against the published root.
The pool type can represent the membership set or explicitly states per-epoch scope.
A regression test mints N VTXOs and verifies all N.

findings.title: Pool payout settlement is an unverified caller assertion
findings.source: Omnia whole-family re-audit (2026-11-17), finding OMN-004
findings.summary: executePoolPayout correctly refuses to settle without evidence, but when `settlement` is supplied it stores it, marks the intent settled-externally, decrements capital and consumes the receipt without checking the evidence. The host casts the RPC parameter to the same type.
findings.impact: A caller with pool-management access can advance accounting as if a payout happened. Whether that is theft depends on who can reach the RPC, but the accounting no longer reflects chain or channel reality.

repro.expected: A settlement object that does not reference the withdrawal id, amount, recipient and pool is rejected and leaves the registry unchanged.
repro.actual: Any object is stored; the intention is marked settled and the receipt consumed.
evidence: packages/omnia-pool/src/withdraw.ts: `if (!params.settlement) return …` then immediate settlement
packages/omnia-host/src/api/methods.ts: `settlement: params.settlement as never`

fix.approach: Verify finality before mutating: for `confirmed` check the transaction against the chain provider and the required depth; for `offchain-final` verify a signed settlement from the channel/factory. Bind the evidence to the exact withdrawal id, amount, recipient and pool.
constraints: No unconditional settlement path, including through the host RPC.
Do not accept a bare boolean or opaque object as finality.
Keep the prepared-draft path unchanged for callers without evidence.
acceptance: Forged or mismatched settlement evidence leaves the registry byte-identical.
A settlement for another withdrawal id, amount, recipient or pool is rejected.
The valid confirmed and offchain-final paths still settle.

findings.title: recordPoolFee trusts a caller-supplied `verified` flag
findings.source: Omnia whole-family re-audit (2026-11-17), finding OMN-005
findings.summary: recordPoolFee forwards `params.verified` into recordLiquidityFee, where earnable records count toward LP entitlement only when `verified === true`. The verifier exists (`feeProofVerifier.verifyFeeProof`) but this path never calls it. claimFees and compoundFees likewise accept any `payoutRef` without confirming it is a settled payout.
findings.impact: A caller trusted to record fees can manufacture verified earnings, or compound them into principal, without establishing that any fee was paid.

repro.expected: An earnable fee record without a verifiable proof cannot increase unclaimed LP fees.
repro.actual: `verified: true` is accepted as-is and the record becomes earnable.
evidence: packages/omnia-pool/src/fees.ts: recordPoolFee passes `verified: params.verified`
packages/liquidity-bond/src/fees.ts: `.filter((r) => !isEarnableSource(r.source) || r.verified === true)`
packages/liquidity-bond/src/fees.ts: the verifier is only used by the separate proof path

fix.approach: Replace the boolean with a verification capability: recordPoolFee either receives a verifier and proof, or records the fee as unverified. Claims and compounds must consume a unique settled payout reference.
constraints: No caller-controlled boolean may gate earnable accounting.
Keep unverified records visible for audit but non-earnable.
Reused payout references must be rejected, not ignored.
acceptance: A forged `verified` flag cannot increase unclaimed fees.
A claim or compound with an unknown or reused payoutRef is rejected.
The verified path still credits the LP.

findings.title: Multi-hop recovery does not journal the outstanding backward preimage duty
findings.source: Omnia whole-family re-audit (2026-11-17), finding OMN-006
findings.summary: revealPreimage fulfils the incoming HTLC (changing signed state) before sending the update to the previous hop. If the send fails, the journal survives — but recover() clears any link whose incoming HTLC is no longer pending, which is now true, so the duty to propagate the preimage backwards is lost. Separately, the host multi-hop RPC throws on failure and discards the router's structured `pendingRefunds`.
findings.impact: A payment can be settled on the outgoing side and never settled backwards, leaving liquidity locked and the payer's HTLC stuck until timeout. Refund obligations are not reported to the caller.

repro.expected: After a failed backward send, restart recovery still knows the preimage must be delivered to the previous hop.
repro.actual: The journal entry is removed because the incoming HTLC is terminal, and the preimage is never retried.
evidence: packages/omnia-relay/src/forwarder.ts: fulfilHTLC then sendMessage then journal.remove
packages/omnia-relay/src/forwarder.ts: recover() clears terminal incoming links
packages/omnia-host/src/api/methods.ts: `throw new Error(result.error)` drops pendingRefunds

fix.approach: Journal distinct states (forward-intent, outgoing-signed, outgoing-accepted, preimage-received, backward-sent, peer-acked, complete) and replay them idempotently on restart. Return pending refunds to the caller on failure instead of dropping them.
constraints: Do not clear a link until the backward settlement is acknowledged or provably terminal.
Replay must be idempotent: no double settlement on repeated recovery.
Keep the journal the single authority; do not infer from channel state alone.
acceptance: A crash after fulfilHTLC but before send leaves recoverable state that retries the backward send.
Repeated recovery never settles the same HTLC twice.
A failed multi-hop call surfaces pendingRefunds to the RPC caller.

origin.note: Partially aliased: the dropped pendingRefunds overlap CAN-022 and the relay journal halves overlap CAN-008/CAN-009. The new part is the durable backward-preimage duty after fulfilHTLC.

findings.title: VTXO claim verification accepts a caller-supplied signer list
findings.source: Omnia whole-family re-audit (2026-11-17), finding OMN-007
findings.summary: The claim policy evaluates membership in `witness.signers: string[]`, which is a list of names, not signatures. The host exposes `omnia/verifyVtxoClaim` and passes `params.signers`, the caller-chosen block height and HTLC status straight through, returning `success: true`.
findings.impact: Any caller can obtain a "valid" claim result by asserting the right names and block. If an operator or integration treats that result as authorisation, a VTXO can be claimed without a signature.

repro.expected: Claim verification requires signatures over the canonical claim preimage and rejects a name list.
repro.actual: `{signers: ["beneficiary"], block: <cliff>}` returns valid without any signature check.
evidence: packages/omnia-vtxo/src/claim-policy.ts: `witness.signers` membership tests
packages/omnia-host/src/api/methods.ts: verifyVtxoClaim passes `params.signers` and `params.block`

fix.approach: Split the policy evaluator from verification. The host must verify signatures over the claim preimage before calling the policy, and take the block from the chain provider rather than the request. Rename the RPC result so it cannot be read as an authorisation.
constraints: Do not accept a signer name list as evidence of a signature.
The block height must come from chain state for the authoritative path.
Keep the pure policy function usable for offline evaluation.
acceptance: A claim with no signature or a wrong signer signature is rejected by the host.
A caller-supplied block that is ahead of the chain tip is ignored or rejected.
The valid signed claim path still succeeds.

findings.title: verifyVtxo accepts a VTXO with no membership proof and never anchors the root
findings.source: Omnia whole-family re-audit (2026-11-17), finding OMN-010
findings.summary: verifyVtxo only checks the proof when `proof.leaf` and `proof.root` are present, and verifyVtxoProof checks the tree against the root carried in the proof itself. Nothing compares that root to the pool's anchored root, and the function never receives the pool.
findings.impact: A VTXO with no proof, or with a self-consistent proof against a root the operator never published, can be reported valid. Combined with OMN-002 there is no current root to anchor against.

repro.expected: A VTXO whose proof root is not the anchored pool root is invalid.
repro.actual: The proof is skipped when absent; when present it is checked only against its own root.
evidence: packages/omnia-vtxo/src/verify.ts: `if (vtxo.proof && vtxo.proof.leaf && vtxo.proof.root)`
packages/omnia-vtxo/src/verify.ts: verifyVtxoProof uses `proof.root`

fix.approach: Take the expected root as a required argument (or a pool/epoch record) and fail closed when the proof is missing or points elsewhere. Keep a separate structural check for offline inspection.
constraints: Missing proof must be an error on the authoritative path, not a skipped check.
Do not silently trust a root supplied by the artifact under test.
acceptance: A VTXO without a proof fails authoritative verification.
A proof against a different root fails.
A valid proof against the anchored root passes.

findings.title: Splice recovery can attach one observed successor to several pending splices
findings.source: Omnia whole-family re-audit (2026-11-17), finding OMN-014
findings.summary: observeSpliceSuccessor matches on address, token and amount and rejects ambiguity within one call, but recoverInterruptedSplices calls it with the same parameters for every pending record, so two pending splices can both adopt the same coin. Nothing binds the observed coin to the splice transaction. The delayed branch also contains `observed ? 'funding_pending' : 'funding_pending'`, a no-op ternary.
findings.impact: A channel can be marked active with a coin that belongs to a different splice, or two records cleared by one coin.

repro.expected: Each pending splice recovers only its own successor.
repro.actual: The same successor observation is applied to every pending record.
evidence: packages/omnia-splice/src/successor.ts: recoverInterruptedSplices loop
packages/omnia-splice/src/successor.ts: no-op ternary in the rebroadcast result

fix.approach: Bind the successor to the splice: require the transaction id or a spent-input link, exclude coins already claimed by another recovery record, and remove the dead ternary.
constraints: Keep the CAN-012 ambiguity rejection.
A coin claimed by one splice must not be reused by another.
acceptance: Two pending splices cannot both adopt one coin.
Recovery either proves lineage or leaves the record funding_pending.

findings.title: Watchtower callbacks only emit observations; nothing protects the channel
findings.source: Omnia whole-family re-audit (2026-11-17), finding OMN-015
findings.summary: lifecycle.ts supplies `onUnilateralClose` and `onHtlcExpiring` handlers that only call `observation.emit`. No contest, protective close or timeout transaction is broadcast, despite the watch service comment saying the host wires these to settlement policy. The successor lookup also matches on address and amount alone.
findings.impact: A unilateral close or an expiring HTLC is noticed but not acted on. The window to contest or claim can pass while the host is healthy.

repro.expected: A unilateral-close finding triggers the contest path (or an explicit, recorded refusal).
repro.actual: Only an observation event is emitted.
evidence: packages/omnia-host/src/lifecycle.ts: both callbacks contain a single `observation.emit`
packages/omnia-host/src/watch.ts: comment claims the host wires contest logic

fix.approach: Implement (or explicitly refuse and surface) the protective action: contest with the latest signed state, timeout or fulfil an expiring HTLC, and record the decision. Make the successor check bind to the channel state rather than address+amount alone.
constraints: Do not claim watchtower support while only emitting events.
A protective action must be idempotent across restarts.
acceptance: A simulated unilateral close causes a contest broadcast (or a recorded, operator-visible refusal).
An expiring HTLC causes timeout/fulfil before the deadline.

findings.title: The initiator discards the peer ERROR frame, so a rejected open reports only acknowledged=false
findings.source: live runs: omnia-open-noncustodial.mjs against Hawk v0.2.12 and v0.3.0
findings.summary: The wire protocol defines an ERROR message carrying payload.error, and the responder sends it with a precise reason. requestPeerReply does receive it, but submitOpenChannel reduces the reply to acknowledged = reply.type === 'ACK' and drops the payload; the integration router has no ERROR branch at all, so the frame is not surfaced anywhere.
findings.impact: Every peer-side rejection is opaque to the caller and to the operator log. In this run the actual cause (funding coin not on chain) only became visible after instrumenting the stream layer on the initiator. Support and automation cannot distinguish a rejected proposal from a lost one without patching the SDK.

repro.expected: The submit result or an observation record carries the responder's reason.
repro.actual: Submit returns { success: true, acknowledged: false } with no reason; nothing is logged unless OMNIA_DEBUG is on, and even then only "[omnia-stream] recv ERROR" with no payload.
evidence: packages/omnia-host/src/api/methods.ts: acknowledged = reply?.type === 'ACK' (reason not read)
packages/omnia/src/integration.ts: _sendError sends payload { error: reason } from 10 call sites
packages/omnia/src/integration.ts: the inbound router switches on CHANNEL_PROPOSAL/STATE_UPDATE/... but has no ERROR case
packages/omnia/src/stream.ts: debug logging prints the message type only
temporary logging-only instrumentation showed: {"error":"acceptChannel failed: Error: Funding coin 0x68778de3... not found on chain"}

fix.approach: Preserve the reason end to end: return it on the submit result (for example acknowledged:false with peerError), include it in the operation record and the observation stream, and handle ERROR explicitly in the integration router so first-contact and routed messages both surface the payload.
constraints: Do not change the ERROR wire format or the reply-matching rules (channelId + nonce).
Do not turn a rejection into a thrown exception where callers already branch on acknowledged.
Do not log secrets from the payload; the reason is a short string.
acceptance: A rejected proposal yields the responder reason to the caller and in the observation record.
The canary can assert on the reason without instrumenting node_modules.

findings.title: Splice successor selection matches on address, token and amount only
findings.source: security audit OMN-NEW-006, verified against source at 8fa26907
findings.summary: observeSpliceSuccessor picks the first unspent coin whose address, token and amount match. Nothing binds the candidate to the splice transaction that created it or to the expected state transition, and the first match wins rather than treating ambiguity as an error.
findings.impact: Two same-value coins at the same script address (a common shape for channel funding addresses) can make the host adopt the wrong coin as the spliced channel. Downstream operations then reference a coin the channel does not control.

repro.expected: The successor is identified by provenance (txid/output index) or ambiguity is rejected.
repro.actual: coins.find(...) on address+token+amount returns the first candidate.
evidence: fix proposed in PR #218 (ambiguous successor is an error)
packages/omnia-splice/src/successor.ts:83 — const candidate = coins.find((coin) => !coin.spent && address && tokenid && amount)

fix.approach: Accept an expected txid/output reference derived from the splice transaction, or read the successor from the spends of the predecessor coin. If more than one candidate matches, fail as ambiguous instead of choosing.
constraints: Do not silently pick a candidate when several match.
Keep the bounded polling and confirmation semantics.
acceptance: Duplicate same-value coins at the address produce an ambiguity error, not a silent pick.
The correct successor is still found in the single-candidate case.

findings.title: Router rollback cannot release HTLCs early and reports failure as if liquidity were returned
findings.source: security audit OMN-NEW-009, verified against source at 8fa26907
findings.summary: On a failed multi-hop payment the router calls timeoutHTLC on each still-pending lock and swallows every error. timeoutHTLC deliberately throws while the chain tip is below the HTLC timeout block, which is the normal case for a payment that just failed. So the rollback releases nothing, yet the failure result and the in-code comment ("stranded HTLCs are never left behind silently") imply it did.
findings.impact: Liquidity stays locked until the timeout block, and callers have no state that says so. A retry can fail for lack of capacity that is not actually gone. This is a recovery-state and API-contract defect, not direct fund theft.

repro.expected: A failed payment records explicit refund-pending locks and releases them once the timeout is valid.
repro.actual: cancelHtlcs catches and ignores the "has not yet timed out" error; the caller sees only a failure.
evidence: fix proposed in PR #218 (pendingRefunds on failure; cancelPayment throws PendingRefundError)
packages/omnia-router/src/execute.ts:52 — try { await ops.timeoutHTLC(...) } catch { /* best-effort */ }
packages/omnia/src/htlc.ts:437 — throw when currentBlock < htlc.timeoutBlock
packages/omnia-router/src/execute.ts:68 — comment claims stranded HTLCs are never left behind

fix.approach: Persist refund-pending locks with their timeout blocks, expose that state in the payment result, and retry when the timeout becomes valid. Distinguish refunded from refund-pending rather than collapsing both into a generic failure.
constraints: Do not claim liquidity was released when timeoutHTLC threw.
Do not bypass the timeout guard to force an early release.
acceptance: A failed payment reports which locks remain pending and until which block.
A retry after the timeout block releases them.
The success path is unchanged.

findings.title: Relay link journal is not atomic and duplicate detection races the write
findings.source: security audit OMN-NEW-010, verified against source at 8fa26907
findings.summary: record() writes the link, then reads the index, then writes the index as a separate operation with no transaction or compare-and-swap. Two concurrent forwards for the same hashlock both pass the duplicate check (which runs before record) and can then both record, with the second index write overwriting the first.
findings.impact: A lost index update hides a link from list()-based recovery, and a duplicate forward creates two outgoing HTLCs for one incoming payment. Both are restart-sensitive and hard to see in logs.

repro.expected: Journal writes are atomic and an incoming HTLC has a single idempotency key.
repro.actual: Two sequential storage.set calls per record; duplicate check precedes the write.
evidence: fix proposed in PR #218 (single-document journal, serialized, upsert by hashlock)
packages/omnia-relay/src/link-journal.ts:47 — storage.set(keyFor(hashlock), link)
packages/omnia-relay/src/link-journal.ts:51 — storage.set(INDEX_KEY, index) (separate write)
packages/omnia-relay/src/forwarder.ts:191 — duplicate check before addHTLC/record

fix.approach: Use one atomic write per link (store the index inside the record, or use a storage transaction), and key idempotency on inChannelId+inHtlcId with a conditional insert. Recover from authoritative records, not from a separately maintained index.
constraints: Do not require a storage adapter feature the published adapters do not have.
Keep list() working for adapters that already hold data.
acceptance: Concurrent record() calls for the same hashlock produce exactly one entry and one outgoing HTLC.
A crash between the two writes cannot lose the link.

findings.title: Funding change goes to the first input owner, and the builder accepts negative output amounts
findings.source: security audit OMN-NEW-011, verified against source at 8fa26907
findings.summary: The CAN-001 fix returns change correctly for a single-owner coin, but two edges remain. With several funding inputs, all excess value is sent to inputAddresses[0] even when the inputs belong to different addresses. In tx-builder, amounts are summed per token and checked against the inputs, but individual negative amounts are never rejected, so a negative output can offset a positive one and still balance.
findings.impact: Multi-owner funding pays the change to the wrong party (and the transaction then cannot be signed by that party alone, so it fails late). The negative-amount gap means a draft can carry an invalid coin amount through conservation checking. Node acceptance of such a transaction was not demonstrated.

repro.expected: Change is returned per input owner, and every amount is required to be a non-negative integer before conservation is evaluated.
repro.actual: Change uses inputAddresses[0] unconditionally; sums() accepts BigInt("-100") and only compares totals.
evidence: fix proposed in PR #218 (mixed-owner funding rejected; negative amounts refused)
packages/omnia/src/transactions.ts:357 — const changeAddress = inputAddresses[0]
packages/tx-builder/src/build.ts:119 — sums() parses amounts with BigInt without a sign check
packages/tx-builder/src/build.ts:136 — only total > available is rejected

fix.approach: Require all funding inputs to share an owner before emitting change, or emit one change output per input address and reject mixed-owner funding with a clear error. In the builder, reject any amount that is negative or not an integer before summing.
constraints: Keep the single-input exact-value path byte-identical.
Do not weaken the existing conservation check.
acceptance: Mixed-owner funding either produces per-owner change or is rejected explicitly.
An output with a negative amount is rejected by the builder.
Offsetting positive and negative outputs cannot pass conservation.

findings.title: Watchtower starts but only observes; it never contests, fulfils or refunds
findings.source: re-audit R-004, verified against source at 5d8c427b
findings.summary: CAN-014 wired the watch service into host start/close and stopped it mistaking updates for closes. Its host callbacks, however, only emit observations: no contest transaction, no HTLC fulfilment or timeout, no refund. A successful close notification also adds the channel to the processed set even though nothing protective ran.
findings.impact: A unilateral close is detected but not answered before the contest deadline, so detection does not protect funds. The processed set can suppress later findings for a channel that is still at risk.

repro.expected: A detected close triggers the protective action and records evidence of completion.
repro.actual: onUnilateralClose emits an observation and the channel is then marked processed.
evidence: packages/omnia-host/src/lifecycle.ts:828-890 — watch callbacks emit observations only
packages/omnia-host/src/watch.ts — closed set updated after the callback resolves

fix.approach: Give the watch service a durable response state machine: explicit contest/fulfil/refund actions, deadline tracking, retries and completion evidence. Only mark a channel processed when the action succeeded.
constraints: Do not mark processed on observation alone.
Do not automate actions the custody mode forbids.
acceptance: A simulated unilateral close produces a contest action before the deadline.
A failed action is retried and never marked complete.
Restart resumes pending responses.

findings.title: Prepared operations bypass the channel lock; refunds are not surfaced by the host; journal is not cross-process safe
findings.source: re-audit R-005, verified against source at 5d8c427b
findings.summary: Three related gaps remain. (1) The shared lock keys on params.channelId, so prepared operations that identify the work by preparedOperationId do not take it (and multi-channel work has no ordered locking). (2) The router now returns pendingRefunds, but the host multi-hop method throws on failure instead of returning that recovery information, and nothing persists a refund queue. (3) The relay journal is a single document per process, but has no storage-level compare-and-swap and does not serialize by incoming HTLC identity.
findings.impact: Concurrent prepared operations can interleave with RPC/peer mutations on the same channel; a failed multi-hop payment loses the refund schedule at the host boundary; two relay processes can lose a journal update.

repro.expected: Prepared, RPC and peer mutations share one lock; failures carry refunds; journal writes are atomic across processes.
repro.actual: Lock lookup ignores preparedOperationId; host throws the router result away; journal has no CAS.
evidence: packages/omnia-host/src/api/methods.ts:3342-3358 — lock key derived only from params.channelId
packages/omnia-router/src/execute.ts — pendingRefunds returned to the caller
packages/omnia-host/src/api/methods.ts — multi-hop handler throws without surfacing pendingRefunds
packages/omnia-relay/src/link-journal.ts — single document, no CAS or per-incoming-key lock

fix.approach: Resolve the channel from the prepared operation before taking the lock; sort multi-channel locks by channelId to avoid deadlock; return pendingRefunds from the host multi-hop method and persist a refund queue; add a compare-and-swap to the journal (revision field) and an idempotency key on inChannelId+inHtlcId.
constraints: Do not serialize unrelated channels.
Do not report a failure as fully refunded.
acceptance: A prepared submission and an RPC call on one channel cannot interleave.
Host multi-hop failures carry pendingRefunds and a scheduled retry.
Concurrent journal writers cannot lose an update.

findings.title: EpochAuthority.append is check-then-act across an await
findings.source: Omnia whole-family re-audit (2026-11-17), finding OMN-009
findings.summary: append() reads current state, checks `spentInputIds`, then awaits `journal.append`. Two concurrent appends for the same input can both pass the check before either writes.
findings.impact: The same VTXO input can be recorded in two epochs, defeating the double-spend guard the journal is meant to provide. Realistic only under concurrent callers in one process or two processes sharing the journal.

repro.expected: Two concurrent appends of the same input: exactly one succeeds.
repro.actual: Both can pass the spent-input check before either append lands.
evidence: packages/omnia-vtxo/src/epoch-authority.ts: `state.spentInputIds.has(inputId)` before `await this.journal.append(event)`

fix.approach: Use an atomic reservation (compare-and-swap on the journal head, or a per-authority serial queue) so the spent set is advanced in the same durable step as the append.
constraints: Do not add a process-local mutex as the only guard; two processes must still be safe.
Preserve the existing signature and epoch ordering checks.
acceptance: Two concurrent appends of the same input: one wins, one throws.
Reopen still shows a single record.

findings.title: Channel graphs advertise every channel that is not closed
findings.source: Omnia whole-family re-audit (2026-11-17), finding OMN-011
findings.summary: The routing provider filters `channel.status === 'closed'`, so funding_pending, quiesced and spliced channels are advertised as routable even though HTLC creation requires `active`. A path can be selected and then fail at lock time.
findings.impact: Routes fail late, after a payment has been attempted; in-flight payments can be stranded.

repro.expected: Only `active` channels appear in the routing graph.
repro.actual: Every status except `closed` is advertised.
evidence: packages/omnia-host/src/router/routing-provider.ts: `if (channel.status === 'closed') continue;`

fix.approach: Filter on the positive predicate (`active`) instead of excluding one terminal status, and share the predicate with the HTLC entry check.
constraints: Do not change channel status values or the wire format.
Spliced channels must rejoin the graph when they return to active.
acceptance: A graph built from mixed-status channels contains only active ones.
A channel that returns to active is routable again.

findings.title: createMultiHopForwarder is exported but never instantiated by the host
findings.source: Omnia whole-family re-audit (2026-11-17), finding OMN-012
findings.summary: The forwarding engine exists in omnia-relay and is exported, but no production host path constructs it. Multi-hop forwarding therefore depends on wiring that the reviewed host does not demonstrate.
findings.impact: The relay package appears supported while the deployed host cannot forward; a two-hop payment has no executing component.

repro.expected: A host started with relay enabled constructs the forwarder and drives it from the channel event stream.
repro.actual: Only the export exists; no host call site.
evidence: packages/omnia-relay/src/index.ts: export only
no createMultiHopForwarder call in packages/omnia-host

fix.approach: Either wire the forwarder into the host lifecycle with a durable journal and expose its state, or mark the package explicitly as a library primitive and remove the implied host support from docs and claims.
constraints: Do not advertise multi-hop as available while it is unwired.
If wired, the journal must be the durable one from OMN-006.
acceptance: Either the host constructs the forwarder and passes an integration test, or the docs and package maturity state that it is library-only.

findings.title: Link journal serialization is in-process only
findings.source: Omnia whole-family re-audit (2026-11-17), finding OMN-013
findings.summary: Journal updates are serialized within one process. The duplicate-forward check runs before signing, so two processes sharing a store can both reserve the same payment.
findings.impact: Two relay processes can both forward one incoming HTLC, producing a double settlement attempt.

repro.expected: Two processes competing for the same hashlock: one forward.
repro.actual: No cross-process reservation.
evidence: packages/omnia-relay/src/link-journal.ts

fix.approach: Reserve atomically in the shared store (CAS on a per-hashlock key) before signing, and release on failure.
constraints: Do not rely on a process-local mutex.
A crashed reservation must be reclaimable after a bounded lease.
acceptance: Two processes: exactly one reservation succeeds.
Expired reservations are reclaimable without double settlement.

findings.title: Channel locking is keyed by the RPC channelId and multi-channel paths escape it
findings.source: Omnia whole-family re-audit (2026-11-17), finding OMN-016
findings.summary: withChannelLock is applied where a channelId is present, but prepared-operation and multi-channel paths can touch several channels without entering a common critical section. Locking on a caller-supplied id also lets a caller serialize against the wrong key.
findings.impact: Concurrent operations on the same channel can interleave through a path that did not take the lock.

repro.expected: Any handler that mutates channel state holds a lock keyed by the channel it derives, not the request.
repro.actual: Some paths take no lock or use the request channelId.
evidence: packages/omnia-host/src/api/methods.ts: withChannelLock call sites
packages/omnia-host/src/channel-lock.ts

fix.approach: Derive lock keys from the resolved channel(s), take them in a stable order for multi-channel operations, and cover prepared-operation commits.
constraints: No deadlock: multi-channel locks must be ordered.
Re-entrancy must keep working.
acceptance: A concurrent test over the same channel cannot interleave.
A multi-channel operation takes both locks in a deterministic order.

findings.title: Factory escape block is derived from the local chain tip
findings.source: Omnia whole-family re-audit (2026-11-17), finding OMN-017
findings.summary: buildFactoryOpening computes `escapeBlock = tip.block + FACTORY_ESCAPE_DELAY_BLOCKS` and puts it in the funding script, while the pending commitment excludes it. Two hosts at different heights therefore derive different scripts for the same proposal, and the finalized terms comparison rejects the opening.
findings.impact: Factories fail to open whenever participants are not at the same tip. This is a liveness defect, not a divergence: the differing script is detected rather than silently accepted.

repro.expected: Both participants derive the same funding script and identity from a proposal.
repro.actual: escapeBlock differs with the tip, so fundingScript and fundingAddress differ.
evidence: packages/omnia-factory/src/factory.ts: `const escapeBlock = tip.block + FACTORY_ESCAPE_DELAY_BLOCKS`
packages/omnia-factory/src/factory.ts: pendingCommitment built without state variables

fix.approach: Derive the escape block from an agreed anchor (the proposal carries it, or it is the funding coin height) and commit to it in the pending commitment so a mismatch is impossible rather than merely detected.
constraints: Do not weaken the escape delay.
The commitment must cover every script-affecting input.
acceptance: Two hosts at different tips derive the same funding script from one proposal.
A changed escape block changes the commitment.

findings.title: 41 publishable packages declare no test:integration gate
findings.source: /Users/peter.cheek/Downloads/CRYSTAL_LABS/TOTEM/totem-sdk/scripts/workspace-gates.config.json
findings.summary: The maturity gate requires test:integration for RC packages, but these declare none and carry no reasoned notApplicable exemption. They are invisible to `verify-workspace --integration`.
findings.impact: A behavioural regression in any of these packages reaches a release with no integration evidence; the canary cannot cover them all on its own.

repro.expected: Every RC package either declares test:integration or a reasoned exemption.
repro.actual: Missing: @totemsdk/agent-policy (rc), @totemsdk/authority (rc), @totemsdk/chain-provider (rc), @totemsdk/connect (rc), @totemsdk/decision (beta), @totemsdk/edge (rc), @totemsdk/governance (rc), @totemsdk/identity (rc), @totemsdk/intelligence (beta), @totemsdk/kissvm (rc), @totemsdk/liquidity-bond (rc), @totemsdk/lookup-client (rc), @totemsdk/lookup-node (rc), @totemsdk/lookup-protocol (rc), @totemsdk/manifest (rc), @totemsdk/mcp-server (rc), @totemsdk/omnia-factory (rc), @totemsdk/omnia-host (rc), @totemsdk/omnia-pool (rc), @totemsdk/omnia-router (rc), @totemsdk/omnia-vtxo (rc), @totemsdk/p2p-hub (alpha), @totemsdk/pear (rc), @totemsdk/provider-bond (rc), @totemsdk/minima-rpc (rc), @totemsdk/pubsub-transport (rc), @totemsdk/qvac (beta), @totemsdk/realtime (rc), @totemsdk/recursive-mast (rc), @totemsdk/root-identity (rc), @totemsdk/se-server (rc), @totemsdk/server (rc), @totemsdk/storage (rc), @totemsdk/stream-transport (rc), @totemsdk/tx-builder (rc), @totemsdk/txpow (rc), @totemsdk/wallet-adapter (rc), @totemsdk/wots-lease (rc), @totemsdk/entity (alpha), @totemsdk/eefi (rc), @totemsdk/replication (alpha)

where: the packages listed in this finding
fix.approach: Add a real test:integration per package (packed-consumer or invariant check), or record a reasoned notApplicable exemption in scripts/workspace-gates.config.json naming an owner.
constraints: Do not add notApplicable entries without an owner and a reason.
Do not add a script that always exits 0.
acceptance: node scripts/verify-workspace.mjs --integration reports no missing test:integration for RC packages.
Each new suite asserts behaviour, not just an import.

findings.title: Two unit suites exceed Jest's 5s default timeout under load
findings.source: canary core exercise: omnia-host prepare-submit-settle, lookup-node lease
findings.summary: The full unit suites fail on a loaded machine because individual tests inherit the 5,000 ms default. omnia-host prepareSettle/submitSettle takes ~15s end to end; lookup-node LEASE_RESERVE passes in 3s alone but exceeds 5s inside the 108s suite. Both pass when given 60s.
findings.impact: CI flakiness and false reds: the suites are green on a fast runner and red on a busy one, so a real regression and a slow machine look identical. It also blocks the canary from exercising these packages as part of a full run.

repro.expected: Both suites pass deterministically.
repro.actual: omnia-host: 1 failed / 125 passed (Exceeded timeout of 5000 ms). lookup-node: 1 failed / 70 passed. Both pass with --testTimeout=60000.
evidence: tests/unit/omnia-host/src/__tests__/prepare-submit-settle.test.ts:20
tests/unit/lookup-node/src/__tests__/lease.test.ts:26
rerun with --testTimeout=60000: 1 passed / 125 skipped, and 1 passed / 70 skipped

fix.approach: Give the specific long tests an explicit timeout that reflects their work (settlement signing and a real lease round-trip), rather than raising the default for every test in the repo.
constraints: Do not set a repo-wide 60s default; it hides genuine hangs.
Do not skip or retry the tests.
acceptance: The full suites pass twice in a row on a loaded machine.
The timeout is scoped to the tests that need it, with a comment saying why.

findings.title: Auto-approval has no mandatory bound (hardening, not a defect)
findings.source: Omnia whole-family re-audit (2026-11-17), finding OMN-018
findings.summary: The gate is deny-by-default and supports both `maxTotalValue` and `allowedPeers`, and both are enforced. `autoApprove: true` with neither bound is still permitted, so an operator can opt into unbounded signing.
findings.impact: A misconfigured unattended host can sign any factory a peer asks for. The default configuration is safe.

repro.expected: Enabling auto-approval without a bound is rejected at construction.
repro.actual: It is accepted; every request is then allowed.
evidence: packages/omnia-host/src/factory-approval.ts: allowedPeers and maxTotalValue are optional

fix.approach: Require at least one bound when `autoApprove` is set, and log the effective policy at startup. Keep the existing defaults and the authorizer hook unchanged.
constraints: Do not change the default-deny behaviour.
Do not make an explicit operator authorizer require the bounds.
acceptance: `autoApprove` without `maxTotalValue` or `allowedPeers` throws at construction.
A bounded policy still auto-approves within its bounds.

origin.note: Downgraded from P2: the gate is deny-by-default and both bounds exist and are enforced. The residual issue is that an operator may opt into auto-approval without a bound; that is configuration hardening, not the unbounded-automation defect the report describes.
